newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Clinton's Asia appeal fits in with U.S. trade push.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's Asia appeal fits in with U.S. trade push.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton's appeal on Wednesday to boost trade with Asia coincides with a host of pacts Washington is pushing in the dynamic region, where the United States suffers some of its biggest trade deficits.

In his State of the Union address, Clinton called for Americans to increase trade with Asia and Latin America, two of the fastest growing regions in the world, "or be left behind as these emerging economies forge new ties with other nations".
Some two million jobs in the United States depended on trade with Asia, he said.
"That is why we need the authority now to conclude new trade agreements that open markets to our goods and services even as we preserve our values..." he said.

He appeared to be talking about China, calling on Congress not to tie his hands in concluding accords with Beijing that range from bilateral trade agreements and China's eventual admission into the world trade body, the World Trade Organisation, to a nuclear non-proliferation treaty.

"Whether Sino-U.S. trade is good or bad is based on whether Sino-U.S. relations are good or bad," Zou Lan, an economist with China's cabinet's State Commission for Restructuring the Economy, told Reuters.
The Clinton administration has already effectively delinked human rights concerns from trade in China under its policy of "constructive engagement" with the world's most populous nation.
That policy has been heartily welcomed in Asia.

"Given that the U.S. and China are Hong Kong's two largest trading partners, a smooth trading relationship between the two countries would certainly benefit Hong Kong," said Edward Leung, chief economist at Hong Kong's Trade Development Council.

The United States and China recently reached an accord on textiles but are still battling over agreements on intellectual property protection and China's reluctance to open its markets to U.S. products.
Asian nations account for much of the U.S. trade deficit.
China's slice of that deficit was expected to swell to $36 billion in 1996 from $34 billion the year before -- the second largest after Japan's.
Even small but rapidly growing Malaysia enjoyed an $8.5 billion trade surplus with the United States in 1995.
U.S. cabinet secretaries and trade diplomats have fanned out across Asia in recent months negotiating various market opening agreements in an effort to redress the balance.
The United States last month reached a landmark "open skies" accord with Singapore, which would allow their airlines virtually unlimited access to each other's countries.
Malaysia said it would sign a similar accord in April.
The pacts could put pressure on Japan to open its skies by giving U.S. airlines alternative hubs in Asia, diplomats said.

Asian countries are key to two other accords -- an Information Technology Agreement (ITA) freeing all trade in computers and telephones by the year 2000 and a pact opening up telecommunications to foreign investment, analysts said.
Japan-U.S. trade friction had been pretty much on the back-burner for a change, partly because of Japan's falling trade and current account surpluses, analysts in Tokyo said.
But if Japan's trade surplus with the United States starts to swell due to the yen's recent slide, friction could heat up again.
"There is going to be trade friction coming up," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia, commenting on the yen's latest decline.
